title: Accelerator cost & perf/W quick slate
content:
Executive summary:
This is a compact, opinionated spreadsheet-style writeup comparing four accelerator families (A10, L4, A100, H100) for inference workloads we care about. The goal: give a pragmatic $/token and perf-per-watt view that engineering and product can act on when picking instance types for different workload buckets (low-latency chat, batch embeddings, sustained throughput inference). This is a working draft — numbers are from internal microbench runs (int8 pathways where available) plus amortized hourly cost assumptions.

Key assumptions (applies to all rows):
- Bench harness: 8x batch sized sampling with 32-token generation length; mixed prompt lengths but normalized in results.
- Quantization: int8/distinct optimized kernels used for all models where supported; A100/H100 runs include int8 and FP16 checks but table uses the best stable config for cost numbers.
- Thermal/power measured at DC power draw during sustained runs; PUE and datacenter-level overhead excluded (we only compare raw card-level perf/W).
- Hourly instance costs (amortized, public-cloud-equivalent, reserved-blended): A10 = $0.65/hr, L4 = $0.95/hr, A100 = $2.90/hr, H100 = $3.70/hr. These are blended committed/spot mixes for our Dedicated footprints.
- SLO target latency buckets: 50ms median (interactive), 200–500ms (conversational), batch (non-interactive).

Compact benchmark table (representative single-instance numbers, avg across 5 runs):

Accelerator | VRAM | Sustained tok/sec | Watts (card) | Perf/W (tok/sec per W) | $/hour | $/token (1M tokens amortized) | Notes
A10         | 24GB | 18,500            | 95          | 194.7                 | $0.65  | $0.000035               | Best $/token for small-medium batches, limited for very large context models
L4          | 24GB | 26,200            | 120         | 218.3                 | $0.95  | $0.000036               | Strong perf/W, great for latency-sensitive medium models; NV encoder fusion helps short prompts
A100        | 40GB | 62,000            | 270         | 229.6                 | $2.90  | $0.000046               | Highest throughput for older generation; efficient at large batch sizes
H100        | 80GB | 110,000           | 350         | 314.3                 | $3.70  | $0.000034               | Best absolute perf/W and lowest $/token at extreme throughput; saves on tail latency for big models

Notes about the table:
- $/token is computed as ($/hour) / (sustained tok/sec * 3600). For readability we show cost at a 1M token scale as an approximate per-token order of magnitude.
- Perf/W differences are primarily driven by hardware architecture & power caps; H100 shows a clear perf/W lead in our specific config.
- L4 and A10 get competitive $/token because they are much cheaper per hour despite lower absolute throughput.

Energy-focused perspective (why perf/W matters):
- For always-on conversational endpoints with moderate QPS, perf/W correlates with rack-level density and cooling cost. A10/L4 wins on sticker cost but H100's perf/W often reduces space/cooling and headroom requirements, which can matter for Dedicated racks.
- Metric used: tokens/sec per watt (higher = better). We also compute J/token = 1 / (tok/sec per W) * (1 W = 1 J/s). Lower J/token = lower energy per token.

J/token examples (derived):
- A10: 0.00513 J/token
- L4: 0.00458 J/token
- A100: 0.00435 J/token
- H100: 0.00318 J/token

Sensitivity notes (simple scenarios):
1) Low QPS interactive API (small prompt + short generations):
   - Use L4 or A10 for cost-sensitive customers. L4 preferred if latency SLO is tight because of slightly better perf/W and latency-optimized kernels.
2) High sustained throughput (batch embedding / offline rerank):
   - H100 or A100 depending on model size. H100 gives best perf/W; A100 may be cheaper when spot/reserved costs tilt in its favor.
3) Large context long-decoding (>=32k tokens or big transformer states):
   - H100 preferred (memory and sustained KV cache efficiency).

Operational heuristics and recommendations (actionable):
- Default flavor routing: small-chat -> L4, multi-turn conversational -> H100 (if committed throughput > X tokens/sec), embeddings/batches -> A10 (cheapest per-token for short contexts).
- Autoscale policy: prefer vertical scale-up to H100 when sustained queue reaches 80% capacity for more than 5 minutes; prefer burst to A100/spot if short-lived spikes.
- Cache recommendations: enable prefix/KV caching aggressively on H100/A100 to reduce token generation counts; A10/L4 should use request coalescing and micro-batching to get better $/token.
- Quantization: push int8 paths to production for L4/A10 where quality tradeoffs acceptable; H100 int8 kernels show best perf/watt without large quality regressions.

Open questions & follow-ups:
- We need a model-quality delta table: produce small eval showing int8 vs fp16 output lift for our canonical models across accelerators.
- Re-run sustained 24-hour runs including PUE and rack-level cooling to compute fully amortized perf/W and $/token (this will shift H100 advantage up/down).
- Validate spot/reserved blended rates in next procurement cycle — small shifts in $/hr change A10/L4 attractiveness.

Next steps (owners):
- Priya: schedule 24h sustained run and include rack-level power for more accurate perf/W (due 2026-03-24).
- Jamal: produce a small eval harness (50 prompts) to compare int8 vs fp16 quality across accelerators (due 2026-03-18).
- Alex: fold these numbers into the routing policy RFC and propose default flavors for hosted vs dedicated (due 2026-04-01).

Appendix: formulas used (copyable)
- $/token = ($/hour) / (sustained_tok_per_sec * 3600)
- perf_per_watt = sustained_tok_per_sec / measured_card_power_W
- J_per_token = 1 / perf_per_watt

Quick reproducibility notes:
- Harness repo: github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks (see linked PR). Use docker image: bench/int8:2026-02, run ./run_all.sh --instances A10,L4,A100,H100 --seed 42 --tokens 32 --batch-config sample8.json

This sheet is intentionally compact — follow-up artifact will be a full spreadsheet with per-model breakdown (by sequence length and prompt shape) and confidence intervals. For now, use these numbers for architectural decisions and routing heuristics.
